children: Rare Pokémon cards continue to outperform traditional assets. The CardTrack 100 index has returned 150.7% since September 2021, beating Bitcoin, gold, and the S&P 500 by wide margins.
The numbers reveal why collectors now treat rare graded cards like serious alternative investments rather than toys.

children: Pokémon Card Values Keep Breaking Records
The CardTrack 100 is a monthly index that tracks the combined value of the 100
worldwide. It works as a thermometer for the top of the collectibles market.
The index currently sits at 251 points, with a base value of 100 set in September 2021. Its total combined value now reaches $244,750 across the tracked cards.
A $5,000 investment made four years ago would be worth $12,534 today based on that performance.
The same capital in Trading View would be worth roughly $ 12,390.
The S&P 500 Trading View even more, returning roughly 73% and turning $5,000 into approximately $8,650 today.
Just twelve days ago on September 29, the index set an all-time high of $253,800 points. The current reading sits only 1.2% below that recent peak.
Why are Collectors Pricing Cards Like Blue-Chip Art?
Mainstream recognition explains the shift. For example, a 1998 Pikachu Illustrator card sold for $16.5 million earlier this year, reshaping the market ceiling permanently.

Recent auctions reinforce the trend. Four rare e-Reader cards, including a Skyridge Gengar, fetched a combined $780,000 this week, while a first-edition Charizard reportedly set a new record of $1.38 million.

eBay executives confirmed that Pokémon was the most searched term in their collectibles category during the first half of 2026. Grading giant PSA reports trading-card games now account for half of its entire business.
Scarcity, professional grading, nostalgia, and a growing class of serious collectors have turned rare Pokémon cards into one of the strongest alternative assets of the decade.

title: Pokémon Cards Just Crushed Bitcoin, Gold and the S&P 500 With 150% Returns
